title: How do you prepare stories for the consulting fit interview?
description: Behavioural questions often count as much as the case. Build 6-8 stories once, and use each for several questions.
hook: You prepare for the fit interview by building six to eight true stories, each told in a clear shape (situation, task, action, result, learning), and rehearsing them out loud until you can tell them naturally and survive follow-up questions. The fit interview is often treated as the easy part, which is exactly why candidates stumble on it. Interviewers want real moments from your life, told clearly and honestly, and a small story bank built once will cover almost any question they ask.
body:
In this guide

  • What firms are looking for
  • STAR-L: the story shape
  • Build a story bank
  • A worked example
  • Make your contribution verifiable
  • Prepare for the follow-ups
  • The other questions to prepare
  • Common mistakes
  • Practise it
  • Where to practise next

What firms are looking for

Most fit questions test the same handful of qualities:

  • Leadership: do people follow you when it is hard?
  • Impact: did things change because of you?
  • Initiative: do you start things nobody asked for?
  • Persuasion: can you bring people round without authority?
  • Resilience: how do you handle failure?

Each firm frames these differently. McKinsey's version is the Personal Experience Interview. As of 2026, its interviewing page asks you to prepare two examples for each area it assesses, including personal impact, entrepreneurial drive and inclusive leadership, and to treat the interview as a conversation rather than a rehearsed story. Expect the interviewer to stay on one story for a long time and keep asking for detail. BCG's interview process page lists integrity, intellectual curiosity, creative thinking, a collaborative mindset and drive. The most common fit questions map neatly onto these qualities.

STAR-L: the story shape

  • Situation: the context, in one or two sentences.
  • Task: what you were responsible for, and why it was hard.
  • Action: what you did, step by step. This is the heart of the story, so say "I", not "we".
  • Result: what changed, with a number if one exists.
  • Learning: what you took from it, or would do differently.

Aim for 90 to 120 seconds per story, told, never read. A useful split for a 105-second story is about 20 seconds on situation and task, 60 on action, 15 on result and 10 on learning. If your situation takes longer than your action, you are spending the interviewer's attention on the part they care least about.

Build a story bank

You do not need a story for every possible question. Write six to eight, then map each to the questions it can answer. One strong story often covers leadership, conflict and impact, if you emphasise a different part each time.

For each story, write four factual anchors: the problem, the decision you owned, what changed and what you learned. Then note one pressure point, the part an interviewer is most likely to dig into, such as a colleague who disagreed with you.

StoryBest forAlso works for
Rescuing a late pricing proposalLeadershipImpact, teamwork
Convincing an operations lead to trial a new schedulePersuasionDisagreement with a senior person
A customer survey launched without a pilotFailureWeakness, learning from feedback
Fixing a sign-up drop-off nobody ownedInitiativeImpact, problem solving

Stories do not have to come from a job. University projects, community work, sport and family responsibilities all work when the details are concrete and your role is clear. Rehearse the full bank out loud once a week.

A worked example

Here is an illustrative leadership story, told in STAR-L. The details are invented to show the shape; use your own.

Situation and task:

In my internship, our four-person team had three weeks to prepare a pricing proposal for a contract worth about $2M a year. With eight days left, the pricing model had errors and our manager was off sick. I was asked to get the proposal over the line.

Action:

I rebuilt the pricing model over a weekend, then split the remaining work by each person's strengths rather than seniority. I went to the account director with a proposal to drop two low-value analyses so we could spend the time checking the numbers that mattered. And I set up a 15-minute daily check-in so problems surfaced early instead of the night before.

Result and learning:

We submitted a day early, and the client accepted our price. What I learned is that cutting scope openly, with the decision-maker's agreement, works far better than asking everyone to work harder.

Every sentence in the action section is something the speaker did. The result is specific, and the learning is a habit, not a platitude.

Make your contribution verifiable

Compare two versions of the same story:

We aligned stakeholders and delivered the launch on time.
Marketing wanted to launch in March and engineering needed until May. I mapped which features customers had asked for most, showed both leads that three of the eight could ship in March, and got them to agree a two-stage launch.

The first leaves the interviewer guessing what you did. The second shows the competing priorities, the evidence you gathered, how you persuaded others and the decision you owned. If several people contributed, say so, then be precise about your part.

Prepare for the follow-ups

Good interviewers take your story apart. Practise answering questions like:

  • "Who disagreed with you, and why?"
  • "What alternative did you reject?"
  • "What would the team have done without you?"
  • "What would you do differently now?"

If you cannot answer these, choose a different story. Never invent a more heroic version: a modest but genuine example will hold up under questioning, and an embellished one will not. A story bank is a memory aid, not a script to recite whatever the question.

The other questions to prepare

Two more answers need the same care as your stories. "Tell me about yourself" should be a 60 to 90 second story with a clear thread; see how to answer it. "Why consulting, and why this firm?" needs specifics: people you spoke to, practice areas, the kind of work you want. The why consulting and why this firm tip covers it.

Common mistakes

  • Too much context. A minute of background before you reach the action. Cut the situation to two sentences.
  • "We" throughout. The interviewer is assessing you. Use "I" for your actions.
  • No number in the result. Time saved, money, people, a grade or a ranking: if a measure exists, use it.
  • Memorised word for word. It sounds recited and breaks under interruption. Learn the anchors, not the sentences.
  • A learning that is not a lesson. "I learned teamwork is important" says nothing. Name the habit you changed.

Practise it

Have a go at each one before you open the answer.

1. Which part of a STAR-L story deserves the most time: situation, action or learning?

Show the answer

Action. The interviewer is assessing what you did, so keep the context short and spend over half your time on your actions.

2. Write the action part of a story about persuading someone you had no authority over, in three sentences that each start with "I".

Show the answer

"I asked the regional head for 20 minutes to understand what worried her about the change. I rebuilt the proposal around her two concerns and ran a two-week pilot in one team so she could see the results. I shared the numbers with her first, before anyone else, so the decision to roll it out was hers."

3. A friend's result reads: "It went really well and everyone was happy." How would you improve it?

Show the answer

Replace the feeling with evidence: what changed, by how much, and over what period. For example, "We cut the report from five days to two, and the team still uses the process." If no number exists, describe an observable change, such as a decision that was made or a process that was adopted.

Where to practise next

Work through the question-by-question articles, starting with the leadership story. Read the McKinsey interview process guide if you are applying there, since its format goes deepest on a single story. Then tell your stories to a partner and ask them to interrupt with follow-ups; the guide to practising with a partner shows how to give each other useful feedback.
outro: This guide is lesson 11 of the free PrepForCase course, where you can do the exercise and quiz and track your progress. Next in this topic: How can you practise case interview thinking in ten minutes a day?
